summary: For ages 10-11, the goal is fluent, flexible movement between fractions, decimals and percentages as three names for one quantity. The load-bearing insight is that the fraction bar means 'divide the top by the bottom', so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Learners should pick whichever form makes a comparison easiest, converting a mixed set to one common form before ordering (e.g. 30%, 1/3, 0.35 → 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35, so the order is 30% < 1/3 < 0.35). Note that 1/3 landing between 30% and 0.35 is counter-intuitive and is where the surface-digit misconception is confronted.
misconceptions: Reverses the division: reads 3/8 as 8 ÷ 3 (divides the larger by the smaller out of habit), giving 2.67 instead of 0.375.
Compares mixed forms by surface digits — thinks 1/3 is largest of {30%, 1/3, 0.35} because '3 is a big number' or because the numbers look bigger, without converting to a common form.
Treats 1/3 as exactly 0.3 (or 0.33) and terminating, not recognising the recurring decimal.
Believes every fraction gives a neat terminating decimal, so is thrown when a division doesn't stop.

activities.title: Watch a fraction become a decimal: 3 ÷ 8
steps: Before dividing, predict: will 3/8 be more than 1 or less than 1, and roughly what? Say why (3 shared among 8 people is less than one whole).
Carry out the division 3.000 ÷ 8 step by step, keeping the decimal point and trailing zeros, to reach 0.375.
Compare the result against your prediction. If you predicted more than 1, check whether you divided 3 by 8 or 8 by 3.
Try a case that never stops: carry out 1 ÷ 3 far enough to see 0.333... keep repeating, and note it does NOT equal 0.3.
Round only when told to (e.g. 1/3 ≈ 0.333 to three decimal places), and explain why the division never terminates.
activities.insight: The fraction bar means 'divide the numerator by the denominator'; 3/8 is 3 ÷ 8, and some divisions (like 1 ÷ 3) produce recurring, non-terminating decimals.

activities.title: Order a mixed set by converting to a common form
steps: Take the set 30%, 1/3 and 0.35. First predict the order smallest→largest by eye, and say why.
Convert all three to ONE common form (decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35), using that percentages are hundredths and division for 1/3.
Plot each converted value on a 0-1 number line and read off the order from position, not appearance.
Compare your conversion-based order (30% < 1/3 < 0.35) with your by-eye prediction and note where they differed — especially whether you expected 1/3 to be biggest.
Transfer the method to a new set, e.g. 30%, 2/5, 0.35: convert each (0.30, 0.40, 0.35) and say where 2/5 goes, and why.
activities.insight: Different forms cannot be reliably compared by surface digits; converting every item to one common form (then plotting on a line) makes the true order visible — and 1/3 sits between 30% and 0.35.

activities.title: Build a landmark equivalence set
steps: For each landmark, show all three names on one shared bar or hundred-grid so the same shaded quantity is seen as fraction, decimal and percentage at once.

Match a form to its partners from memory (e.g. given 1/5, recall 0.2 and 20%); for fractions that are not landmarks, rewrite them as tenths or hundredths where easy (e.g. 3/20 = 15/100), and otherwise use division.
Note which landmarks are exact and which (like 1/3) are recurring, so you don't record 1/3 as a terminating 0.33.
activities.insight: Memorised landmark equivalents let you convert common cases instantly, reserving division for less familiar fractions, while a shared visual shows the three forms name one quantity.

checkQuestion: Convert 3/8 to a decimal and show how you got it. Then take 30%, 1/3 and 0.35, put them in order from smallest to largest, and tell me how you compared them.
checkAnswer: 3/8 = 0.375, found by dividing 3 ÷ 8. Order: 30% < 1/3 < 0.35 (i.e. 0.30 < 0.333... < 0.35), compared by converting all three to the same form — decimals: 0.30, 0.333..., 0.35.
